```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# fill-in table drawn with base graphics so row height is controllable;
# body = list of rows, each a list/vector of cell strings ("" = blank)
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    fnt <- if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val,
                                    font = if (is_ans) 3 else fnt, cex = cex,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. Emits nothing in non-LaTeX output. lines =
# lines of prompt text, rows = rows of blank space below it (0.3 in each),
# extra = any other height (in inches), e.g. a code block
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}

model_rows <- list(c("A", "temp", "2.5"), c("B", "temp, bullfrogs, canopy", "2.5"),
                   c("C", "all eight", "2.5"), c("D", "all eight", "0.3"))
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
f1 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 2)
```

```{r fits, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# the WOD's code, run as written (with the missing line filled in)
options(cmdstanr_no_ver_check = TRUE)
library(cmdstanr)
ponds <- read.csv("../../data/BdRegionalSurvey.csv")
X_all <- scale(as.matrix(ponds[, 2:9]))
pond_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] X;
  array[N] int<lower=0> n_frogs;
  array[N] int<lower=0> n_pos;
  real<lower=0> prior_sd;
}
parameters {
  real b0;
  vector[K] beta;
}
model {
  b0 ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  beta ~ normal(0, prior_sd);
  n_pos ~ binomial_logit(n_frogs, b0 + X * beta);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  for (i in 1:N)
    log_lik[i] = binomial_logit_lpmf(n_pos[i] | n_frogs[i], b0 + X[i] * beta);
}
"
pond_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(pond_code))
fit_ponds <- function(cols, s) {
  pond_model$sample(
    data = list(N = nrow(ponds), K = length(cols), X = X_all[, cols, drop = FALSE],
                n_frogs = ponds$frogs_swabbed, n_pos = ponds$bd_positive,
                prior_sd = s),
    chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0, show_messages = FALSE)
}
loos <- list(A = fit_ponds(1, 2.5)$loo(), B = fit_ponds(c(1, 7, 3), 2.5)$loo(),
             C = fit_ponds(1:8, 2.5)$loo(), D = fit_ponds(1:8, 0.3)$loo())
comp <- loo::loo_compare(loos)
```

```{r answers}
est <- t(sapply(loos, function(l) c(l$estimates[c("elpd_loo", "p_loo", "looic"), "Estimate"],
                                     max_k = max(l$diagnostics$pareto_k))))
diff_of <- function(m) comp[m, c("elpd_diff", "se_diff")]
runner_up <- rownames(comp)[2]
```

**NRES 746, Week 10, Lecture 2: Comparing Pond Models with LOO (take-home)**

&nbsp;

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta sans-serif type; longer answers have a bar in the margin.}

**Due Monday.** This uses the 60-pond survey from Lab 8 and the Stan
setup from last week's take-home. Fitting all four models takes a few
minutes.

**Using AI:** each coding question is labeled with a recommendation.
After each one, circle how you actually used AI.

**What to turn in:** your filled-in answers and a screenshot of your

## Part 1: The model

Here is Lab 8's logistic-binomial model in Stan. `X` holds whichever
standardized predictors you pass in, and `prior_sd` sets the width of
the Normal(0, `prior_sd`) prior on every slope. To compute LOO, Stan
must also save the **log-likelihood of each pond** at every draw, in
`generated quantities`. One line is missing.

```{r stan-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
library(cmdstanr)
ponds <- read.csv(
  "https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/BdRegionalSurvey.csv")
X_all <- scale(as.matrix(ponds[, 2:9]))   # temp, elev, canopy, cond, area,
                                          # fish, bullfrogs, road

pond_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] X;
  array[N] int<lower=0> n_frogs;
  array[N] int<lower=0> n_pos;
  real<lower=0> prior_sd;
}
parameters {
  real b0;
  vector[K] beta;
}
model {
  b0 ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  beta ~ normal(0, prior_sd);
  n_pos ~ binomial_logit(n_frogs, b0 + X * beta);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  for (i in 1:N)
    log_lik[i] = ____________________________________ ;
}
"
pond_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(pond_code))

# fits the model with the predictor columns in `cols` and prior SD `s`
fit_ponds <- function(cols, s) {
  pond_model$sample(
    data = list(N = nrow(ponds), K = length(cols), X = X_all[, cols, drop = FALSE],
                n_frogs = ponds$frogs_swabbed, n_pos = ponds$bd_positive,
                prior_sd = s),
    chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0)
}
fit_b <- fit_ponds(c(1, 7, 3), 2.5)   # Model B: temp, bullfrogs, canopy
loo_b <- fit_b$loo()
loo_b
```

`r nq(4, 4)`

**1a.** *(Recommended: no AI.)* Fill in the missing line. (Hint: the
`model` block's likelihood, for pond `i` only. Stan's `_lpmf` functions
use a bar: `f_lpmf(y | parameters)`.) Then run the code.
**Check:** Model B's `looic` should be close to 221.8.

\ansbegin

`log_lik[i] = binomial_logit_lpmf(n_pos[i] | n_frogs[i], b0 + X[i] * beta);`

\ansend

AI use (circle one): no AI / AI helped (e.g., debugging) / AI wrote the code

`r nq(3, 3)`

**1b.** Why does LOO need the log-likelihood of each pond separately,
rather than one total for all 60?

\ansbegin

LOO scores how well the model predicts each pond when that pond is left
out, so it needs each pond's own contribution; a single total can't be
split back into ponds. (It also gives a Pareto $k$ for each pond.)

\ansend

`r nq(6, 0, extra = 2.7)`

## Part 3: Interpret

**3a.** Is the best model clearly better than the runner-up? Use
`elpd_diff` and `se_diff`.

\ansbegin

No. Model `r rownames(comp)[1]` is best, but runner-up `r runner_up` is
behind by only `r f1(-diff_of(runner_up)[1])` with an SE of
`r f1(diff_of(runner_up)[2])`, about one SE: within noise. Model A, by
contrast, is `r f1(-diff_of("A")[1])` behind (SE `r f1(diff_of("A")[2])`),
clearly worse.

\ansend

`r nq(4, 5)`

**3b.** Models C and D have the same eight predictors. Why is D's
`p_loo` (the effective number of parameters) smaller, and why might it
predict new ponds better?

\ansbegin

D's narrow prior holds every slope near 0 unless the data push it away,
so the slopes can't move freely and the model behaves as if it had
fewer than its nine parameters (`p_loo` `r f1(est["D", 2])` vs. `r f1(est["C", 2])`). Less
freedom means less fitting of noise, so predictions for new ponds
improve (here elpd `r f1(est["D", 1])` vs. `r f1(est["C", 1])`).

\ansend

`r nq(4, 5)`

**3c.** Compare the LOO ranking with the AIC table from Lab 8 Act 1.
What does LOO tell you that AIC didn't?

\ansbegin

Same story: temperature + bullfrogs + canopy is best, all eight
predictors do a little worse, and temperature alone is far behind.
Model B's LOOIC (`r f1(est["B", 3])`) is close to its AIC (221.16). LOO
adds an SE for each difference, a per-pond check of the approximation
(Pareto $k$, all at or below `r f2(max(est[, 4]))` here, well under 0.7), and it works for Model D, where a
prior makes "number of parameters" unclear for AIC.

\ansend

`r nq(3, 3)`
